source_title: Unlawful Use of an Unmanned Aircraft System; Law-Enforcement Mitigation Authority
citation: La. R.S. 14:337 (originally enacted 2014 La. Acts No. 661, eff. Aug. 1, 2014; most recently amended by 2025 La. Acts No. 23, §1, and 2025 La. Acts No. 170, §1 [HB 261, the "We Will Act" Act], eff. Aug. 1, 2025)
revision_date: 2025-08-01 (2025 La. Acts No. 170 and No. 23); prior amendments 2024 La. Acts No. 19; 2021 La. Acts No. 265, eff. 2021-06-14; 2016 La. Acts No. 529, eff. 2016-06-17, and No. 539; original enactment 2014 La. Acts No. 661
uas_topic: UAS-facilitated surveillance/privacy of "targeted facilities" (petrochemical, nuclear, school, grain, and R.S. 14:61(B) critical-infrastructure sites); governor's-mansion and correctional-facility overflight restriction; military-installation overflight restriction; law-enforcement counter-UAS mitigation authority
regulated_party: Any person operating a UAS, including private and commercial operators; law enforcement officers/agencies (subsection G mitigation authority only)
regulated_activity: Using a UAS to conduct surveillance of, gather evidence or information about, or photographically/electronically record a "targeted facility" without the owner's prior written consent; flying a UAS over the governor's mansion or a state/local correctional facility without the facility head's written consent; surveilling, interfering with, or recording a federal or state military installation without the commander's written consent; and, for law enforcement, detecting, tracking, intercepting, or disabling a UAS operating in a "nefarious manner"
requirement_type: Prohibition (Subsection A), with an enumerated consent-based and FAA-compliance exception structure (Subsections C-D, F), plus an affirmative law-enforcement mitigation-authority grant (Subsection G)
permit_or_approval_required: No state permit process for private/commercial operators; the operative protections are the property owner's, correctional-facility head's, or military-installation commander's prior written consent, or falling within a statutory exception
public_agency_only: No (Subsections A-F regulate any person, including commercial operators; Subsection G's mitigation authority is limited to law enforcement officers/agencies)
aec_relevance: Yes — directly bears on aerial mapping, inspection, and construction-monitoring UAS work near refineries, chemical/rubber manufacturing plants, nuclear generation facilities, grain elevators, schools, and R.S. 14:61(B) critical infrastructure, which by its own terms extends to active construction/improvement sites of such infrastructure
summary: La. R.S. 14:337(A) makes it unlawful to intentionally use a UAS to conduct surveillance of, gather evidence or information about, or photographically/electronically record a "targeted facility" without the owner's prior written consent (subject to escalating misdemeanor/felony-range penalties and mandatory forfeiture on repeat or aggravated violations under Subsection E); to fly a UAS over the governor's mansion or a state/local jail, prison, or juvenile/adult correctional facility without the facility head's written consent; or to surveil, interfere with, or record a federal or state military installation without the commander's written consent. "Targeted facility" (Subsection B(6)) means petroleum/alumina refineries, chemical/rubber manufacturing facilities, nuclear power generation facilities, schools (as defined in R.S. 14:40.6(B)), grain elevators/storage, and "critical infrastructure" as defined in R.S. 14:61(B) — a cross-referenced definition that lists 7 categories (chemical/manufacturing/refinery, electrical generation/transmission, water intake/treatment, natural-gas/LNG/pipeline, port/rail/pipeline/trucking transportation, water-control structures, and communications/data facilities) and, notably, expressly extends to "any site where the construction or improvement of any facility or structure referenced in this Section is occurring." Subsection C exempts a property owner (and third persons the owner retains) from the surveillance prohibition on the owner's own property or property held under a lease/servitude/right-of-way/permit/license. Subsection D exempts any UAS operator acting in compliance with FAA regulations/authorization, persons engaged in agricultural commercial operations (R.S. 3:41), and university-sanctioned research/teaching UAS use. Subsection F exempts authorized motion-picture/television production filming. A 2025 amendment (Act 170, HB 261, the "We Will Act" Act) added Subsection G, authorizing a law enforcement officer or agency to take "reasonable and necessary mitigation measures" — detection, tracking, identification, and interception/disabling via jamming, hacking, or physical capture — against a UAS operating within Louisiana in a "nefarious manner," where there is reasonable suspicion of criminal activity, an imminent public-safety threat, or another state/federal-law violation.
verification_status: Full current text verified directly against the official Louisiana State Legislature website (legis.la.gov), including the complete Acts amendment history line; cross-checked against Justia's parallel 2025-currency reproduction (law.justia.com), which matched verbatim. The 2025 Act 170/HB 261 enrollment, effective date (Aug. 1, 2025), and "Signed by the Governor. Becomes Act No. 170" status were independently confirmed via the bill's official legis.la.gov BillInfo history page. R.S. 14:61(B)'s cross-referenced critical-infrastructure definition (including the construction-site extension in (B)(1)(b)) was independently verified in full directly against legis.la.gov/Justia.
notes: CITATION-ACCURACY NOTE: several secondary drone-law aggregator sites describe R.S. 14:337 using only its 2014-2021 penalty structure (fines up to $500/$1,000) and omit the 2024-2025 additions (governor's-mansion and military-installation provisions, the Subsection G mitigation authority, and the escalated felony-range penalties for the military-installation violation under Subsection E(5), which carries up to 5 years at hard labor and a $2,000-5,000 fine) — those secondary summaries describe stale, pre-2024 law. The Subsection G mitigation authority (the "We Will Act" Act, effective Aug. 1, 2025) makes Louisiana the first state to grant state/local law enforcement direct UAS-mitigation authority (jamming, hacking, or physical capture), per contemporaneous reporting from the Governor's Office and multiple trade-press outlets; this is a materially different and more operationally significant posture than most states' UAS statutes, which do not authorize non-federal actors to disable third-party aircraft. AEC firms operating near petrochemical, refinery, or other 'targeted facility' sites in Louisiana (a state with an unusually dense petrochemical/industrial corridor) should independently confirm that mitigation measures under Subsection G are directed only at UAS reasonably suspected of criminal or unsafe activity, not at compliant commercial Part 107 operations, though the statute does not expressly exempt compliant commercial flights from Subsection G's mitigation-authority trigger the way Subsection D exempts them from the Subsection A prohibitions.

source_title: Regulation of Unmanned Aerial Systems and Unmanned Aircraft Systems; Preemption
citation: La. R.S. 2:2 (created 2017 La. Acts No. 238, §1, eff. June 14, 2017; amended 2021 La. Acts No. 328, §1)
revision_date: 2021 La. Acts No. 328 (amendment date within 2021 session); original enactment 2017-06-14
uas_topic: State preemption of local UAS/UAS-aerial-system regulation
regulated_party: State government (exclusive regulatory jurisdiction); political subdivisions and local units of government (regulatory authority preempted)
regulated_activity: Any political subdivision or other unit of local government enacting a rule, regulation, code, or ordinance regulating unmanned aircraft systems or unmanned aerial systems
requirement_type: Preemption (field preemption of local UAS regulation), subject to the federal government's exclusive sovereignty over airspace under 49 U.S.C. 40103
permit_or_approval_required: N/A — this is a jurisdictional-allocation statute, not a permit program
aec_relevance: Yes — establishes that no Louisiana parish or municipality may impose an independent UAS operating rule, permit, or ordinance; a commercial AEC operator need only clear state and federal requirements, not a patchwork of local drone ordinances
summary: La. R.S. 2:2(A) provides that, subject to Subsection C and except as otherwise provided by law, the state has exclusive jurisdiction to regulate all unmanned aircraft systems and unmanned aerial systems, and that state law supersedes and preempts any rule, regulation, code, or ordinance of any political subdivision or other unit of local government. The section expressly disclaims any effect on the federal government's exclusive sovereignty over U.S. airspace under 49 U.S.C. 40103, and states that any interpretation contradicting federal UAS regulatory authority is null. Subsection B defines "unmanned aerial system" and "unmanned aircraft system" (the latter excluding satellites, and UAS used by federal/state government contractors, local law-enforcement/fire agencies, and utility/cable/telecom/rail entities regulated by the Public Service Commission, a local franchising authority, the FCC, or the Federal Railroad Administration while performing facility operation/repair/maintenance work). Subsection C provides that if federal law preempts any provision of this section, that provision is null.
verification_status: Full current text verified directly via Justia's 2025-currency Louisiana Revised Statutes reproduction (law.justia.com), which displays the complete Acts history (2017 creation, 2021 amendment) matching the citation found in secondary reporting; the official legis.la.gov codified-statute page for this specific section was not independently re-opened in this pass (legis.la.gov's statute-lookup tool required a document ID not resolved during this research pass), so this record is verified to the Justia-reproduction level for the statutory text itself, though the Acts numbers and effective date are corroborated by multiple independent secondary sources (law-firm summaries, drone-law guides) describing the same 2017 Senate Bill 69 origin.
notes: Secondary sources commonly (and correctly, per this verification) attribute this preemption framework to 2017 Senate Bill 69, which is consistent with the 2017 La. Acts No. 238 citation found directly on Justia; no discrepancy was found here, in contrast to several other findings in this research pass. Note the statute preempts political-subdivision *regulation* of UAS operation; it does not by its terms prevent a local government from imposing generally applicable rules of conduct for its own publicly owned property (e.g., a city park's launch/land rules) — that distinction is drawn by secondary commentary rather than the statute's text itself, and is flagged here as an interpretive question for a future phase rather than asserted as settled law.

summary: LAC 76:III.113(A) provides that "operation of drones or unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV) is prohibited on department-administered lands including wildlife refuges and wildlife management and habitat conservation areas." The rule is promulgated under the LDWF Secretary's general property-management authority (R.S. 56:5) and the Wildlife and Fisheries Commission's rulemaking authority (R.S. 56:109), and contains no stated exception, permit process, or research/law-enforcement carve-out within this specific section.

source_title: General and Wildlife Management Area Hunting Rules and Regulations — Aircraft/Drone-Assisted Taking and Wounded-Game Recovery
citation: La. Admin. Code tit. 76, Part XIX, §111(D)(5) and (D)(14) (promulgated under R.S. 56:115 and related Title 56 hunting-regulation authority)
effective_date: Unknown (exact original promulgation date of D.14 not independently verified; in force as of the 2025-2026 hunting-regulations digest)
revision_date: 2025-2026 regulations digest (current); a Notice of Intent amending D.14 for the 2026-27/2027-28 seasons was passed by the LWFC on Feb. 5, 2026, with public comment accepted through March 6, 2026, and had not been confirmed as finally adopted/published as of this research date
status: Current / in force, with a material pending amendment (see notes)
regulated_party: Any person (licensed hunters and the general public)
regulated_activity: Currently: using an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)/drone to aid in the recovery of a wounded deer or bear (D.14), and, more broadly, taking game quadrupeds or birds from aircraft or participating in the taking of deer with the aid of aircraft (D.5, not UAS-specific but covering manned-aircraft-assisted takings)
requirement_type: Prohibition (D.14, currently absolute for wounded-game recovery by drone; D.5 covers aircraft-assisted taking generally)
permit_or_approval_required: No permit process under the current D.14 text (flat prohibition); the pending NOI amendment would introduce an FAA-certification and operational-restriction framework rather than a permit
commercial_operator_relevance: Yes — limited to hunting-related UAS activity, not general commercial UAS use, but directly relevant to any AEC-adjacent land-management or wildlife-survey UAS work conducted in conjunction with hunting-lease or WMA operations
summary: LAC 76:XIX.111(D)(14) currently states: "Use of Drones for the Recovery of Wounded Deer or Bear. The use of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV) (commonly referred to as a drone) to aid in the recovery of a wounded deer or bear is prohibited." Separately, D.5 prohibits "[t]aking game quadrupeds or birds from aircraft or participating in the taking of deer with the aid of aircraft or from automobiles or other moving land vehicles," a general (not UAS-specific) restriction that predates and reinforces the drone-specific rule and mirrors the federal Airborne Hunting Act of 1956. On February 5, 2026, the Louisiana Wildlife and Fisheries Commission (LWFC) passed a Notice of Intent (NOI) amendment to D.14 for the 2026-27 hunting regulations that would permit FAA-certified operators to use a drone to locate (but not take) a mortally wounded deer or bear outside official hunting hours, using lights/infrared to confirm the animal is not alive and healthy, with no weapon-mounting and a requirement to leave the area immediately and not relay coordinates to hunters if a live, healthy animal is found. As of this research date, LDWF's own Feb. 12, 2026 announcement confirmed the amendment was at the NOI/public-comment stage (comment period through March 6, 2026, plus a Feb. 26, 2026 public Zoom hearing), not yet confirmed as a finally adopted rule published in the Louisiana Register.
verification_status: The current D.14/D.5 rule text was verified directly via Cornell LII's Louisiana Administrative Code mirror (law.cornell.edu), which reproduces the full official LAC Title 76, Part XIX, §111 text; a parallel Justia reproduction (regulations.justia.com) was independently identified but not separately re-opened given the size of this section. The pending NOI amendment status was verified directly against LDWF's own Feb. 12, 2026 news release (wlf.louisiana.gov) and a Feb. 5, 2026 Louisiana Illuminator news report (a named, dated, primary-adjacent government-sourced news outlet), which together confirm the amendment had passed the NOI stage but remained in a public-comment/pending-final-adoption posture as of those dates; final Register publication/adoption was not independently confirmed in this pass.
notes: MATERIAL CURRENCY FLAG: at least one secondary AI-generated search summary reviewed during this research pass described the wounded-game drone-recovery rule as already "passed"/"now permitted for the 2026-27 season" based on the LWFC's Feb. 5, 2026 NOI vote; this conflates NOI passage (a preliminary step opening a public-comment period) with final rule adoption and Register publication. Per LDWF's own release, the NOI comment period ran only through March 6, 2026, and the news coverage reviewed described the change as merely "likely becoming official before the fall 2026 hunting season" opens — not yet confirmed final as of this research date. AEC/land-management firms and hunting-lease operators should independently confirm current Register-published status with LDWF before relying on any wounded-game drone-recovery exception; the flat D.14 prohibition should be treated as the current binding rule absent that confirmation.

summary: The Louisiana Office of State Parks' Field Memo 2018-001 ("Drone Use Guidelines," dated March 5, 2018) states that operation of unmanned aircraft systems, including drones, on Office of State Parks property is regulated by the FAA and relevant state and local laws, and that drone users shall adhere to the policy and comply with FAA regulations, state and federal law, and other applicable local laws/policies. The memo assigns department heads and supervisors responsibility for assisting in implementation, complying with the rules, regulations, and spirit of the applicable FAA Certificate of Authorization, and communicating the policy to employees under their direction. Secondary sources report that Louisiana does not have a blanket, statewide administrative ban on recreational drone flights at state parks, and that individual parks may apply additional site-specific rules; this project did not independently verify site-specific rules for any individual park.

regulated_activity: DOTD's webpage directs operators to FAA drone registration, "Know Before You Fly," and FAA UAS resources; the Advisory Committee studies and reports on UAS industry conditions, legal barriers, and FAA/state/local coordination, and appoints an FAA liaison member

aec_relevance: Yes — DOTD's UAS Advanced Air Mobility program (LIFTOff Louisiana, tied to federal Executive Order 14307) and the Advisory Committee's designated Louisiana Society of Professional Surveyors seat both signal active state engagement with the surveying/AEC UAS industry, though neither currently imposes binding operator requirements
summary: DOTD's Office of Multimodal Commerce, Aviation Division states its UAS-related goal is to ensure drones and UAS operate safely in Louisiana airspace, and its public UAS webpage primarily links out to FAA drone registration, the "Know Before You Fly" campaign, and FAA UAS resources rather than stating independent state operating rules. Separately, La. R.S. 2:2.1 creates the Louisiana Advanced Aviation and Drone Advisory Committee within DOTD, a fifteen-member body with designated seats for, among others, the Louisiana Farm Bureau Federation, DRONERESPONDERS Public Safety Alliance, the Louisiana Society of Professional Surveyors, the Louisiana Mid-Continent Oil and Gas Association, the Pelican Chapter of AUVSI, two academic institutions, and the Houma-Terrebonne Airport Commission. The committee must meet at least quarterly, issue an annual pre-session report on Louisiana's UAS industry (legal barriers, operator counts, commercial users, economic value, comparative state ranking, and FAA actions), and appoint a member to liaise with the FAA on federal/state/local UAS law issues. DOTD separately promotes a Houma-Terrebonne-based "UAS Gulf of Mexico Center of Excellence" for highly automated large-UAS (L-UAS) operations, and a 2026 federally selected "LIFTOff Louisiana" Advanced Air Mobility project tied to federal Executive Order 14307 ("Unleashing American Drone Dominance").

R.S. 2:2.1's full current text (including the committee membership list, reporting duties, and Acts history) was verified directly via Justia's 2025-currency reproduction. The L-UAS Commission/Houma-Terrebonne Center of Excellence and "LIFTOff Louisiana"/Executive Order 14307 references were identified via a Louisiana Division of Administration policy memo and DOTD program pages but were not independently verified section-by-section in this pass; they are included as contextual, lower-confidence background rather than as independently verified binding authority.
notes: Neither the DOTD webpage nor R.S. 2:2.1 imposes a binding operator-facing UAS requirement; this record is included because it documents the state's institutional UAS-policy infrastructure (relevant to an AEC firm tracking Louisiana's regulatory trajectory) rather than because it currently regulates commercial UAS operations. The Advisory Committee's initial member terms were set to run through the 2026 Regular Session per the statute; whether new appointments have been made was not confirmed in this pass.

summary: La. R.S. 37:682 defines "practice of land surveying" to include the measuring of areas, land surfaces, streams, bodies of water, and swamps for correct determination and description; the establishment, reestablishment, ascertainment, or description of land boundaries, corners, divisions, distances, and directions; the plotting and monumenting of lands and subdivisions; and "mapping and topographical work." Unlike Kentucky's analogous statute, the Louisiana definition located in this pass does not contain an express reference to "photogrammetric" control or any other sensor/method-specific term; it is framed generally around surveying activities and outputs rather than the equipment or platform used to produce them. No standalone LAPELS rule, advisory opinion, or FAQ specifically addressing UAS-derived photogrammetric or LiDAR survey products, or governing when UAS-collected data constitutes the practice of land surveying, was located during this research pass.

Firms should confirm directly with LAPELS whether any board policy, informal guidance document, or continuing-education material addresses UAS-derived deliverables before relying on this citation for a specific project; LAPELS's full Board Rules (Title 46, Chapter 27) were not reviewed section-by-section in this pass and may contain relevant material not captured here.

summary: No Louisiana Governor executive order, Louisiana Attorney General opinion, or Louisiana state-court decision directly and dispositively addressing UAS regulation was located in this research pass. Governor Jeff Landry has issued an executive order restricting state-agency use of Chinese-developed generative-AI platforms, but no located executive order specifically addresses UAS/drone procurement or operation. On state-agency UAS procurement: 2024 Regular Session House Bill 915 (Rep. John Wyble) would have prohibited using public funds to procure "prohibited" Chinese-manufactured UAS (defined by reference to the federal American Security Drone Act of 2023) and required the Governor's Office of Homeland Security and Emergency Preparedness to maintain a "cleared" UAS vendor/product list; the bill's official legis.la.gov history shows it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, considered at a May 1, 2024 committee hearing, and shows no further recorded action (no committee report, no floor vote, no enrollment) — meaning it died in committee and was never enacted into law. No Louisiana statute imposing an enacted state-agency UAS procurement/country-of-origin restriction was located; the only current UAS-related procurement framework applicable in Louisiana is the federal American Security Drone Act of 2023, to the extent it independently binds federal-funds recipients. No statute expressly preempting local UAS ordinances beyond La. R.S. 2:2 (LA-002, which does address preemption directly) was separately identified as a distinct authority.
verification_status: HB 915's full legislative history (bill text, committee referral, May 1, 2024 committee consideration, and absence of any subsequent action) was verified directly against the official Louisiana Legislature BillInfo page (legis.la.gov), which is the authoritative record of a bill's status.
